title: Opinion: Montana’s ‘right to try’ law makes patients responsible for bearing costs — and risks
summary: Montana has become the first state to have its own ‘right to try’ law, but important questions remain, researchers write.
content: In July, Montana became the first state to license clinics to offer patients who are not terminally ill drugs and devices that the Food and Drug Administration has not approved. Supporters call state Senate bill 535 a first-in-the-nation expansion of the “right to try.” Critics say it lets patients, including medical tourists from other states, pay out of pocket for unproven therapies. They are both right, in different ways. While the expansion of access to experimental treatments may provide patients with hope, the risks that patients may pay high costs for ineffective and even unsafe treatments remain high. The goal is to expand access to experimental therapies, with stem cell, anti-aging therapies, and biologics being likely use cases. But the law leaves major questions unanswered: How much will patients pay? Who will bear the cost if complications arise later? And, because these therapies are being used outside a rigorous research setting, how will anyone know whether they actually work? For patients, a primary concern is likely to be cost. SB535 makes patients financially responsible for the experimental treatment — with the price set by the company supplying the drug or device. The required patient agreement must describe “all the anticipated costs” of the treatment itself. But patients will likely face additional costs, including travel to Montana for those out of state, and follow-up care. Read the rest…

title: Pregnancy is the ‘perfect storm’ for eating disorders, but doctors keep missing them
summary: Many women struggle with eating disorders before and after childbirth, but they often slip through the cracks of the U.S. health care system.
content: Reporting for this story was supported by the Pulitzer Center . REISTERSTOWN, Md. — Katye Jorgensen had been fighting anorexia and bulimia for years when she got pregnant at 25. Weigh-ins at prenatal appointments filled her with dread and certain foods terrified her, but she powered through for her baby’s sake. Then she struggled to breastfeed her son and lose weight after giving birth, and her mental health deteriorated. Read the rest…
